interest: This file is particularly interesting to historians for two distinct reasons. First, it documents the acute diplomatic friction between the United States (SCAP) and its Pacific allies—principally Australia—over the unilateral American decision to revive the Japanese Antarctic whaling fleet in late 1946 to combat severe domestic and global food and fat shortages, despite Australian security anxieties and opposition to Japanese maritime expansion. Second, the file contains a notable archival anomaly: an unsent five-page State Department telegram from March 1946 concerning copyright protection and the status of prewar intellectual property treaties in occupied Japan (specifically the 1905 U.S.-Japan Copyright Convention and the Berne Convention) that was erroneously bound into decimal file 894.628/894.528, offering valuable insight into occupation legal policy regarding wartime abrogation of bilateral treaties.
overview: This file from State Department decimal classification 894.628 (and stamped 894.528) primarily concerns occupation policy regarding the authorization and diplomatic fallout of the 1946–1947 Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition, as well as an unrelated, misfiled State Department draft telegram regarding copyright protection in occupied Japan. The whaling documents comprise an internal State Department memorandum detailing the legal, economic, and security justifications prepared to answer formal Australian protests against SCAP-authorized Japanese whaling in the Antarctic, along with War Department correspondence coordinating cable traffic to SCAP. The file also includes a misplaced March 1946 draft telegram from the State Department to SCAP examining whether the 1905 U.S.-Japan copyright convention remained in force following the war and directing that American copyright holders receive interim most-favored-nation treatment under Japanese law comparable to Berne Convention signatories.

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum formulating arguments to counter Australian government protests against SCAP's authorization of a Japanese whaling expedition to the Antarctic.
subfiles.summary: John M. Allison provides Assistant Secretary of State John H. Hilldring with key points to refute Australian objections to the SCAP-authorized Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition. The memorandum contends that SCAP acted within administrative authority under Directive 20A to alleviate critical domestic and global shortages of fats and oils, with all produced oil subject to International Emergency Food Council allocation. It stresses that SCAP enacted stringent security precautions—including accompanying American observers, intelligence screening of Japanese crews, and a 12-mile exclusion zone from non-Japanese territory—while affirming that long-term whaling rights and the conversion or reparation of Japanese vessels remain subject to future Allied consultation.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum from John M. Allison to General John H. Hilldring Regarding Answer to Australian Protest on Japanese Whaling in the Antarctic

subfiles.about: War Department letter advising that a proposed cable to SCAP on the Antarctic whaling expedition is redundant due to prior State Department dispatches.
subfiles.summary: Major General Oliver P. Echols of the War Department's Civil Affairs Division responds to Assistant Secretary Hilldring's memorandum regarding a proposed cable to SCAP about the Antarctic whaling expedition. Echols reports that State Department Telegram 544 had already transmitted the identical subject matter to SCAP on November 1, 1946, and that SCAP had already responded on November 4 via cable C66891. Consequently, the War Department determines that transmitting the proposed duplicate cable is unnecessary.
subfiles.title: Letter from Major General O. P. Echols to Assistant Secretary of State J. H. Hilldring Concerning Proposed SCAP Whaling Cable

subfiles.about: Unsent State Department telegram providing policy instructions to SCAP on American copyright protection in occupied Japan and the legal status of the 1905 bilateral copyright convention.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Frank A. Schuler, Jr.)
subfiles.summary: This unsent State Department telegram instructs SCAP regarding legal queries on the continued validity of the November 10, 1905 U.S.-Japan copyright convention and interim protection for American copyright holders. The Department observes that the prewar convention disadvantageously allowed Japanese publishers to print unauthorized translations of American works, whereas Berne Convention signatories received full protection in Japan. Rather than taking a definitive legal position on whether wartime hostilities terminated or suspended the 1905 treaty prior to a final peace conference, the Department authorizes SCAP to issue an interim directive to the Japanese government granting American works unconditional most-favored-nation copyright protection on terms no less favorable than those accorded to Berne Convention members.
subfiles.title: Unsent Draft Telegram from Department of State to SCAP Tokyo on Copyright Protection in Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP), Tokyo
